title: The lion and the mouse
hook: a spared mouse later gnaws the lion free from a net (Aesop)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hare napped and the tortoise kept walking. Your line was slow and steady. What small step did you take? Day sixty-six.

A flat tire on the highway. A night in the hospital. A week when everything falls apart. The help that shows up in a pinch is often not who anyone would have guessed. Not the important friend, not the boss, not the one with the big job. It's the neighbor you barely knew. The quiet coworker. The stranger. Aesop has a fable about exactly that, and it starts with a lion asleep in the sun. A little mouse, running about, doesn't look where it's going, and runs right across the lion's face. The lion wakes up, and his huge paw comes down. Today's story is the lion and the mouse.
screen: `WHO HELPED IN A PINCH?` → `NOT WHO YOU'D HAVE GUESSED.` → `A MOUSE ON A LION'S FACE.`

segments.voice: The mouse is pinned. It's about to be eaten. And it begs: please, let me go. Spare me, and one day I'll repay you. The lion finds this hilarious. A mouse, repay a lion? What could something that small ever do for him? But he's amused, and not very hungry, so he lifts his paw, and the mouse runs off. Some time later, the lion is hunting in the forest and walks straight into a trap: a hunters' net. The ropes close around him. He struggles, and the more he struggles, the tighter it holds. He roars, and roars, and the whole forest hears it. So does the mouse. It runs to the net, looks it over, and starts to gnaw. One rope. Then another. Its teeth are tiny, but they're sharp, and it doesn't stop until there's a hole big enough, and the lion walks out free. And the mouse says, more or less: you laughed at me when I said I'd repay you. Now you know even a mouse can help a lion. Two things are going on. First, the obvious one: don't judge who can help you by their size. Small friends matter. Second, look at the lion's kindness. He didn't spare the mouse as an investment. He laughed at the very idea of being repaid. He let it go for nothing, and that's exactly the kind of kindness that comes back in ways nobody could plan. You can't know which small, unrepayable kindness will turn out to be a rope someone gnaws through for you one day. So here's one way to carry it: be kind to the small ones anyway.
screen: `SPARE ME, AND I'LL REPAY YOU.` · `THE LION LAUGHS, AND LETS GO.` · `THE MOUSE GNAWS THE NET.` · `KINDNESS WITH NO PLAN.` · then, large: `SMALL FRIENDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be kind to someone who can't repay you. For now, settle, and breathe. Think of the people around you whose help you've never counted on. The kid next door. The person who cleans the office. The new member of the group. Someone older, or younger, or quieter. Pick one. Think of one small kindness you could offer them today, with no thought of getting anything back. Like the lion, just lift the paw. The bell holds the time.
The lion and the mouse. A lion spares a mouse, laughing, and the mouse later gnaws him free from a hunter's net. Today's word.
screen: `THE LION AND THE MOUSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: small friends. Today, do one kindness for someone who seems too small to matter, and expect nothing back. Day sixty-six.

options: eat it; a mouse can't repay a lion.

original.note: Greek: the lion and the mouse, as the fable is titled in Greek collections.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cute story about a mouse paying back a favor.
what it means: don't judge who can help by their size, and be kind to the small with no plan to be repaid.
what a scholar hears: a Greek fable (Perry 150); the lion's kindness is a joke to him, which is what makes it free.

notes: Fable paraphrased (Townsend 1867 not quoted). Details (the lion not very hungry; the mouse's closing words) vary by version.
Perry 150 and Greek λέων καὶ μῦς: confirm.

Editor review (days 58-75 pass): hook no longer opens "Think of"; "the fable's advice" now framed as one way to carry it (the Greek moral is about the strong needing the weak); "told for over two thousand years" and "one of Aesop's best-known" removed.
